stimuli.title: Scenario: a woman with COPD who cannot catch her breath
stimuli.text:
Dispatch, 0710: a 71-year-old woman with trouble breathing. En route, dispatch adds that she uses home oxygen at 2 L/min.

She sits in a kitchen chair leaning on the table, breathing through pursed lips. Her husband says she has COPD, has coughed up green sputum for 3 days and has used her inhaler every hour since last night.

stimuli.title: Scenario: a motorcycle rider down
stimuli.text:
Dispatch, 1530: motorcycle versus car on a two-lane road. Police are on scene and traffic is stopped.

A 24-year-old man lies 15 feet from his motorcycle, helmet on, awake and moaning. Bright red blood is spurting from a deep wound on his left thigh and pooling under him.

stimuli.title: Scenario: a wheezing 4-year-old
stimuli.text:
Dispatch, 2140: a 4-year-old boy with trouble breathing.

He sits upright on the sofa, leaning forward, with wheezing you can hear from the door. His mother says he has asthma and a cold, and he has used his inhaler twice in the last hour without relief. He weighs about 16 kg. The children's hospital is 12 minutes away; an ALS unit is 15 minutes out.

stimuli.title: Scenario: a man down in a restroom
stimuli.text:
Dispatch, 1215: an unresponsive man in a fast food restaurant restroom. Police have cleared the scene.

A man about 30 years old lies on the floor with a syringe and a bent spoon near his hand. He is breathing about 4 times a minute with snoring sounds, and his lips are blue.

stimuli.title: Scenario: early morning chest pain
stimuli.text:
Dispatch, 0545: a 61-year-old man with chest pain. No ALS unit is available; you are the highest level on the call, and a PCI center is 25 minutes away.

He is pale and sweaty on the couch and has had crushing chest pressure and nausea for 40 minutes. He has high blood pressure and smokes.

stimuli.title: Scenario: an older woman more confused than usual
stimuli.text:
Dispatch, 1100: an 84-year-old woman at an assisted living facility is "more confused than usual."

Staff say she has been treated for a urinary infection for 3 days and stopped eating yesterday. She has dementia and heart failure. She weighs about 60 kg.

stimuli.title: Scenario: a reaction at a restaurant
stimuli.text:
Dispatch, 1930: a 35-year-old woman with an allergic reaction at a restaurant.

She learned after eating that her dish contained shrimp. She has hives across her chest, swollen lips and says her throat feels tight. She weighs about 70 kg and has no auto-injector with her.

stimuli.title: Scenario: a crash with several patients
stimuli.text:
Dispatch, 1645: a van and a pickup have collided on a county road. Your unit, with you and one EMT, is the first to arrive.

You count six patients. Three are walking around. One is screaming with an open lower leg fracture. One is lying in the road breathing fast. One is slumped in the van and not moving.

stimuli.title: Scenario: sudden trouble speaking
stimuli.text:
Dispatch, 0820: a 71-year-old woman "can't talk right," per her husband.

She woke at 0600 feeling normal and ate breakfast. At 0745 her coffee cup fell from her right hand and her speech became garbled; her husband saw it happen. She has atrial fibrillation and high blood pressure.

stimuli.title: Scenario: a baby on the way at home
stimuli.text:
Dispatch, 0310: a woman in labor at home, 40 minutes from the nearest hospital.

She is 29, in her third pregnancy and at full term. Contractions are 2 minutes apart, her water broke an hour ago with clear fluid, and she says she has to push.

questions.stem: An unresponsive adult has a glucose of 44 mg/dL and an IV line. What should you give?
options: Glucagon IV push, then oral glucose
One full liter of saline first
D10 in small doses, up to 25 g
Oral glucose gel in the cheek
questions.explanation: NASEMSO treats glucose of 60 mg/dL or less with IV dextrose given in increments, D10 preferred, to a field maximum of 25 g. Oral glucose needs a patient who can protect the airway, and glucagon is the option when no IV is possible.

questions.stem: Which form of aspirin does NASEMSO prefer for suspected acute coronary syndrome?
options: Dissolved in a full glass of water
questions.explanation: Chewable, non-enteric-coated aspirin is absorbed fastest; an enteric coating delays release until the tablet passes the stomach. The dose is 162 to 325 mg.

questions.stem: After placing a supraglottic airway, which finding best confirms that the lungs are being ventilated?
questions.explanation: A square, repeating capnography waveform shows exhaled CO2 with each breath, which only happens when air reaches the lungs. Oxygen saturation lags behind by minutes, and tube fogging or quiet epigastric sounds can mislead.

questions.stem: Place the steps for packing a deep, bleeding wound high in the groin in order.
options: Hold firm pressure over the packing
Keep packing until it is full
Push gauze into the wound's depth
Wrap a pressure bandage over it
Expose and find the bleeding point
questions.explanation: Packing works only when gauze reaches the bleeding vessel, so find the source, feed gauze deep, fill the wound, hold firm pressure and then bind it. A tourniquet cannot fit above a wound this high.

questions.stem: How many mL of 10 percent dextrose contain 25 g of dextrose?
questions.explanation: D10 holds 10 g in every 100 mL, so 25 g takes 250 mL. The same 25 g is 50 mL of D50 or 100 mL of D25.

questions.stem: For each disclosure of patient information, specify whether HIPAA permits it.
rows: Abuse report required by state law
His name to a TV reporter
questions.explanation: Sharing information for treatment, and reports the law requires, are permitted. Telling the media, posting photos or informing an employer without the patient's authorization are not.

questions.stem: A 15 kg child with low blood sugar has no IV access. What glucagon dose fits?
questions.explanation: NASEMSO gives 0.5 mg IM or IN to children under 20 kg (or under 5 years) and 1 mg to those 20 kg or more. 3 mg is the dry-powder nasal product's dose, not an IM dose for a small child.

questions.passage: RR 30, HR 112, BP 152/88, SpO2 84% on her home oxygen, temperature 38.1 C. Wheezes in all fields and quiet bases. Barrel-shaped chest. She speaks 3 to 4 words at a time and is alert.
questions.stem: For each finding, specify whether it needs action now or fits her usual baseline.
rows: Speaking 3 to 4 words at a time
questions.explanation: A saturation well below her usual on home oxygen, short phrases and a rate of 30 show she is failing to keep up. A barrel chest and daily home oxygen are part of her chronic disease.

questions.stem: Which explanation best fits her presentation?
options: COPD flare from a chest infection
questions.explanation: Three days of colored sputum and fever on top of COPD, with wheezing and a falling saturation, point to an exacerbation triggered by infection. Nothing here suggests a sudden clot or a cardiac cause.

questions.stem: Which treatments fit now? Select two.
options: Stop all oxygen to be safe
questions.explanation: A bronchodilator nebulizer opens her airways, and her oxygen is raised to a modest target. Lying flat makes breathing harder, and stopping oxygen in a hypoxic patient is never safe.

questions.passage: After two nebulizer treatments she is drowsy and hard to rouse. RR 10, SpO2 92%, ETCO2 72 mm Hg with a sloping waveform.
questions.stem: What do her new findings most likely mean?
options: She is falling asleep from relief
questions.explanation: Drowsiness with a slow rate and an ETCO2 of 72 mm Hg means she is no longer moving enough air and CO2 is rising. A better saturation alone does not show better ventilation.

questions.stem: What should you do for her now?
options: Let her rest and recheck later
questions.explanation: A drowsy patient who is not ventilating needs breaths from a BVM with oxygen, timed to her own effort. CPAP needs an alert patient who can protect her airway.

questions.stem: Which detail about her oxygen is most useful to the receiving hospital?
options: Her usual home flow and saturation
The brand of her oxygen tank
questions.explanation: Knowing her normal flow and usual saturation lets the team set her target and judge how far she is from baseline. The equipment details do not change her care.

questions.stem: A man with chest pain took tadalafil for erectile dysfunction last night. What about nitroglycerin?
options: Give it if SBP is over 90
questions.explanation: Nitrates are avoided within 48 hours of a phosphodiesterase inhibitor such as tadalafil or sildenafil, because together they can drop the blood pressure dangerously. A smaller dose or another form does not remove that risk.

questions.stem: Oral glucose should not be given to a diabetic patient who:
questions.explanation: Oral glucose is for a conscious patient with a patent airway who can swallow. A low reading, mild confusion or an insulin pump do not stop it; a patient who cannot swallow may aspirate.

questions.stem: Capnography on a patient with wheezing shows a rounded, sloping upstroke like a shark fin. This pattern suggests:
questions.explanation: A slow, sloping rise in exhaled CO2 means air leaves the lungs slowly through narrowed bronchioles, as in asthma or COPD. A flat line suggests a displaced device, and a rising baseline points to rebreathing.

questions.stem: A 60 kg adult has burns over about 30 percent of the body and is not in shock. Using the Rule of 10, what is the starting fluid rate in mL per hour?
questions.explanation: The Rule of 10 multiplies the burned percentage, rounded to the nearest 10, by 10 for adults of 40 to 80 kg: 30 x 10 = 300 mL per hour. Add 100 mL per hour for each 10 kg over 80 kg.

questions.stem: A man with pinpoint pupils is breathing 4 times a minute and is blue. What comes first?
questions.explanation: NASEMSO puts airway and breathing support before naloxone: oxygenate with a BVM, then give naloxone. Waiting for the drug to work leaves him hypoxic, and a glucose check comes after ventilation.

questions.stem: The hospital reads your transmitted 12-lead as an inferior STEMI. BP is 98/62. What fits best?
questions.explanation: Inferior infarcts often involve the right ventricle, which depends on preload, and NASEMSO gives nitroglycerin only when SBP is over 100. A second aspirin adds nothing, and an upright position lowers preload further.

questions.stem: Which mask should you wear for a patient with suspected tuberculosis?
options: No mask if he coughs into a tissue
questions.explanation: Tuberculosis spreads through airborne droplet nuclei, so the crew needs a fitted N95 or higher respirator; a surgical mask goes on the patient if he can tolerate it.

questions.stem: When titrating IV naloxone for an opioid overdose, what is the goal?
questions.explanation: Naloxone is given to restore breathing, not to wake the patient completely. Large doses that wake him fully can bring on sudden withdrawal, vomiting and agitation.

questions.stem: How does CPAP help a patient with acute pulmonary edema?
options: It replaces the need for oxygen
questions.explanation: Steady positive pressure splints the alveoli open so oxygen can cross, reduces the work of breathing and lowers the return of blood to the congested lungs.

questions.stem: Which findings suggest an acute stroke? Select three.
options: One side of the face droops
questions.explanation: Sudden facial droop, arm drift and slurred speech are the core stroke screen findings. Bilateral cramps, fever with a stiff neck and hiccups point elsewhere.

questions.stem: Place the steps for acquiring and sending a 12-lead ECG in order.
options: Clean and dry the skin sites
Explain it and position him supine
questions.explanation: Explain and position first, prepare the skin so the electrodes stick, place limb leads then precordial leads, record while the patient is still, and transmit early so the receiving center can activate its team.

questions.stem: A stab wound to the abdomen has left the radial pulse absent and SBP 80. How much fluid should you give?
options: A single 2 L bolus right away
None until he is in surgery
questions.explanation: Trauma resuscitation aims for an SBP near 90 mm Hg, a palpable radial pulse or an alert patient, given as 500 mL boluses. Pushing higher dilutes clotting factors and can restart bleeding.

questions.stem: For a suspected stroke, which time matters most to report?
options: When she last ate a meal
questions.explanation: Treatment windows are measured from the last time the patient was known to be normal. Time found can be hours later and would falsely shorten or lengthen the window.

questions.stem: What is your first action?
questions.explanation: Spurting arterial bleeding kills in minutes, so a tourniquet high and tight on the thigh comes before anything else, including airway checks in a patient who is talking. Vitals and spine care follow.

questions.passage: The tourniquet has stopped the bleeding. HR 128, BP 86/54, RR 24, SpO2 95%. Skin pale and cool. Pupils equal and reactive. His left thigh is deformed and painful.
questions.stem: With the bleeding controlled, specify whether each finding is a sign of shock.
questions.explanation: A fast pulse, pale cool skin and a low pressure show blood loss the body can no longer make up for. Reactive pupils and thigh pain are findings, but not signs of shock.

questions.stem: He is breathing well and talking. What should you do about his full-face helmet?
options: Have him take it off himself
Cut the strap and tip it back
Pull it off before moving him
Leave it on; hold the head
questions.explanation: A helmet that fits and does not block the airway can stay on, with the head kept still, until the airway needs access. Removing it roughly can move an injured neck.

questions.stem: Which destination fits best?
questions.explanation: A systolic pressure under 90 and a thigh wound needing a tourniquet are field triage criteria for the highest level of trauma center available. A small hospital may have to transfer him.

questions.passage: After 500 mL of saline: radial pulse present, BP 94/60, alert. Blood is seeping from beneath the tourniquet.
questions.stem: After a 500 mL bolus his radial pulse returns, but blood is oozing again from under the tourniquet. What should you do?
options: Loosen it to check the wound
Tighten it or add a second one above
Remove it and use a pressure dressing
questions.explanation: As pressure improves, a tourniquet that was just tight enough may start to leak. Tighten it, or place a second one above it; never loosen one to inspect the wound in the field.

questions.stem: Which radio report best prepares the trauma team?
questions.explanation: A short structured report of age, mechanism, injuries, vital signs, treatment and arrival time lets the team activate. Details of the vehicle or social history can wait for the handoff.

questions.stem: A paramedic on scene asks you to push IV midazolam for a seizure. What should you do?
options: Give it, since he is senior
Say it is outside your scope
Call medical direction and give it
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines are not in the AEMT scope model, and neither a senior provider's request nor a radio order widens your license. Offer the help you can give, such as airway support, and let the paramedic give the drug.

questions.stem: Before calling a stroke alert, which test should you do on scene?
questions.explanation: Low blood sugar can cause one-sided weakness and slurred speech that clears with dextrose, so NASEMSO checks glucose in every suspected stroke.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old is breathing 6 times a minute with a strong pulse. How often should you give a BVM breath?
questions.explanation: Children who need assisted ventilation with a pulse get a breath every 2 to 3 seconds, 20 to 30 a minute. Every 6 seconds is the adult rate, and faster breaths cause gastric distension.

questions.stem: Where does the V1 electrode go?
questions.explanation: V1 sits in the fourth intercostal space just right of the sternal border and V2 mirrors it on the left. The fifth space at the midclavicular line is V4.

questions.stem: An 18 kg child is wheezing with hives and vomiting after eating cashews. What IM epinephrine dose fits?
questions.explanation: NASEMSO gives 0.15 mg of 1 mg/mL epinephrine IM in the thigh to children under 25 kg and 0.3 mg to patients 25 kg or more.

questions.stem: For an adult with a serious head injury, NASEMSO advises keeping the SBP above:
questions.explanation: Even one episode of low blood pressure worsens brain injury, so the target for a head-injured adult is above 110 mm Hg, higher than the 90 mm Hg used for other bleeding trauma.

questions.stem: Signs of anaphylaxis persist after the first IM epinephrine dose. When can it be repeated?
questions.explanation: IM epinephrine may be repeated every 5 to 15 minutes while signs of anaphylaxis and poor perfusion persist, alongside a 20 mL/kg fluid bolus if perfusion is poor.

questions.stem: During CPR, ETCO2 reads 8 mm Hg and has stayed there for several minutes. What does this most likely show?
options: The patient has a pulse again
The airway device is in the esophagus
questions.explanation: During CPR, ETCO2 reflects the blood flow compressions create, and readings under about 10 mm Hg suggest poor compressions, so push harder and faster and change compressors. A waveform that is present shows the airway is in place.

questions.stem: Place the steps for inserting a supraglottic airway in an apneic adult in order.
options: Oxygenate with a BVM and adjunct
Lubricate the back of the device
Size the device to the patient
Slide it along the hard palate
questions.explanation: Oxygenate first so the attempt does not cause hypoxia, then choose the size, lubricate, insert along the palate until resistance, confirm with waveform capnography and secure it so it cannot move during transport.

questions.stem: For each patient, specify whether the findings fit anaphylaxis or a simple allergic reaction.
rows: Hives only after a new soap
Hives and wheezing after a sting
Itchy eyes and sneezing in spring
Lip swelling and vomiting after peanuts
questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis involves two or more body systems, or low blood pressure after exposure. Hives alone or itchy eyes and sneezing involve one system and are a simple allergic reaction.

questions.stem: Who is responsible for the protocols an EMS agency's AEMTs follow?
questions.explanation: Every EMS clinician practices under a physician medical director, who writes or approves the protocols and standing orders and oversees quality review.

questions.stem: An adult with suspected sepsis has a MAP of 58. How does NASEMSO guide the fluids?
options: A slow rate of 100 mL per hour
Fluids only if SBP falls below 70
questions.explanation: Adults in septic shock get rapid boluses, such as 500 mL, toward a MAP of 65, up to about 30 mL/kg unless pulmonary edema develops. Waiting for a lower pressure delays care, and a MAP of 100 is not the goal.

questions.passage: RR 44, HR 150, SpO2 89%. Retractions between the ribs and above the collarbones. He speaks two words at a time and watches his mother.
questions.stem: Which findings are most worrying? Select three.
options: Speaking only 2 words at a time
questions.explanation: Low saturation, retractions and short phrases show severe distress in a child. Being alert is reassuring for now, and a mild fever and runny nose explain the trigger, not the danger.

questions.stem: Which treatment fits first?
questions.explanation: A child with bronchospasm who is still breathing on his own needs a bronchodilator nebulized with oxygen. BVM breaths are for a child who is tiring out, and antihistamines do not open the airways.

questions.stem: His mother wants to hold him during the treatment. What is best?
options: Hold the mask on him firmly
Ask her to wait in the kitchen
Lay him flat on the stretcher
questions.explanation: A calm child breathes more easily, and sitting up in a parent's lap is the best position for him. Separating him or forcing a mask on him makes him cry and breathe harder.

questions.passage: Ten minutes later his wheezing is barely audible. RR 16, drowsy, SpO2 84%.
questions.stem: What does this change most likely mean?
questions.explanation: A quiet chest with a slow rate, drowsiness and falling saturation in a child who was working hard means he is running out of energy and moving little air. It is not improvement.

questions.stem: What should you do now?
questions.explanation: A child who is tiring needs assisted ventilation with a BVM and oxygen, timed to his own breaths if he still has any. Letting him sleep invites respiratory arrest.

questions.stem: Where should this child go?
questions.explanation: With a deteriorating child, waiting 15 minutes for ALS on scene loses time when a pediatric center is 12 minutes away. Start transport and let ALS meet you if they can.

questions.stem: A scalp wound is bleeding briskly over a spot where the skull feels soft. How should you control it?
questions.explanation: Pressure directly on a possible depressed skull fracture can push bone fragments inward, so press around the edges with a bulky dressing. Scalp wounds bleed heavily and do need control.

questions.stem: Which findings allow you to withhold resuscitation in a pulseless adult? Select three.
questions.explanation: Rigor mortis, dependent lividity and decomposition are signs of obvious death in NASEMSO's guidance. Cold skin, fixed pupils and a missing pulse occur in arrests that can still be reversed, so resuscitation starts.

questions.stem: An older adult has a fever. Which findings raise concern for sepsis? Select three.
questions.explanation: A fast respiratory rate, new confusion and low blood pressure are signs that an infection is affecting the whole body. A normal saturation, heart rate and glucose do not add to the concern.

questions.stem: Which finding makes a nasopharyngeal airway a poor choice?
questions.explanation: Clear fluid from the nose after head trauma suggests a skull base fracture, and a nasal airway could pass through it. A gag reflex, clenched teeth and snoring are reasons a nasal airway is chosen.

questions.stem: A seizure that continues without stopping is status epilepticus once it has lasted about:
questions.explanation: NASEMSO treats seizure activity lasting more than 5 minutes, or seizures without recovery between them, as needing active treatment. Waiting 15 or 30 minutes risks brain injury; benzodiazepines are given by ALS.

questions.stem: An adult in cardiac arrest now has a supraglottic airway. How should breaths be given?
questions.explanation: Once an advanced airway is in, compressions continue without pauses and one breath is given every 6 seconds. The 30:2 pause is for BVM ventilation without an advanced airway.

questions.stem: Online medical direction orders a drug over the radio. What prevents an error?
options: Write it down after the call
questions.explanation: Echoing the drug, dose and route back to the physician confirms the order was heard correctly before you give it. Writing it later or acting before confirming invites errors.

questions.stem: A farm worker sprayed with pesticide is drooling, wheezing and has pinpoint pupils. What is in AEMT scope?
questions.explanation: The scope model lets every level use auto-injector antidotes for chemical exposures. Titrating IV atropine is a paramedic skill, and albuterol does not reverse the excess secretions.

questions.stem: After you seal a chest stab wound, the patient becomes more short of breath and his BP falls. What should you do?
options: Place a second dressing on top
Lift the dressing to vent air
Lay him flat on that side
questions.explanation: Rising distress after an occlusive dressing suggests air trapped under pressure. Briefly lifting a corner lets it escape; needle decompression is a paramedic skill, so call for ALS as you transport.

questions.stem: A family is found sleeping in a garage with a running generator. Why might pulse oximetry mislead you?
options: Cold fingers make it read high
questions.explanation: Standard pulse oximeters cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so a poisoned patient may show a normal SpO2. Cold fingers usually cause a failed or low reading, not a falsely high one.

questions.stem: A runner is confused and hot after a race, temperature 41.2 C. What is the priority?
questions.explanation: Altered mental status with a high core temperature is heat stroke, and cooling quickly, ideally by cold water immersion, is the treatment that saves the brain. Oral fluids are unsafe in a confused patient.

questions.stem: An alert patient with acute pulmonary edema has BP 188/104. Which drug best lowers preload?
questions.explanation: Nitroglycerin dilates veins and pools blood away from the lungs, and it pairs with CPAP in hypertensive pulmonary edema. A fluid bolus adds to the congestion, and albuterol treats bronchospasm.

questions.stem: A hypothermic patient with a slow pulse is found in snow. How should he be moved?
options: With his legs rubbed for warmth
questions.explanation: A very cold heart is irritable, and rough handling can trigger ventricular fibrillation. Move the patient gently and horizontally and do not rub the limbs.

questions.stem: Before kneeling beside him, what is the main hazard to deal with?
options: A risk of fire in the room
questions.explanation: NASEMSO notes opioids do not give off vapor that harms rescuers unless aerosolized; the real risk is a needlestick. Look for and secure sharps, and wear gloves.

questions.stem: Place your first actions for this patient in order.
questions.explanation: Open the airway, place an adjunct for the snoring, and breathe for him with oxygen before naloxone, as NASEMSO advises. Then reassess, since naloxone takes minutes to work.

questions.passage: With BVM ventilation started, capnography shows a clear waveform with an ETCO2 of 68 mm Hg.
questions.stem: What does the first ETCO2 of 68 mm Hg show?
options: The airway is in the esophagus
questions.explanation: A value well above 45 mm Hg means CO2 has built up from slow, shallow breathing. A good waveform also shows air is reaching the lungs, so the airway is working.

questions.passage: After IV naloxone he breathes 14 times a minute, is groggy and rouses to voice.
questions.stem: He is breathing 14 times a minute and is groggy. Why keep watching him closely?
options: His pupils will widen too far
questions.explanation: Many opioids last longer than naloxone, so breathing can slow again after the dose wears off. Repeat checks of rate, depth and ETCO2 catch it early.

questions.stem: For each finding, specify whether it is a sign of withdrawal or an effect of the opioid.
questions.explanation: A large naloxone dose can cause sudden withdrawal with vomiting, agitation, sweating and gooseflesh. Small pupils and slow breathing are the opioid itself.

questions.stem: He wakes, is angry and says he is leaving. What is the best approach?
options: Hold him down until police arrive
questions.explanation: A patient who has just been revived may still lack capacity. Assess his decision-making, explain that the overdose can return, and involve medical direction and police if he cannot safely refuse.

questions.stem: At a large incident run under the Incident Command System, where do arriving ambulances usually report?
questions.explanation: Units report to staging and wait for an assignment, which keeps the scene from clogging with vehicles and lets command send each crew where it is needed.

questions.stem: During a breech birth the body has delivered, but the head has not. What should you do?
options: Make an air space with a V of fingers
Pull firmly on the baby's legs
questions.explanation: NASEMSO has you place a gloved hand in the vagina with two fingers forming a V on either side of the baby's face to keep an air space, while you prepare for rapid transport. Never pull on the body.

questions.stem: A toddler strapped in a harnessed car seat needs spinal motion restriction after a crash. How is he removed?
options: Still strapped in the car seat
Lifted out onto a long board
questions.explanation: NASEMSO extricates infants and toddlers already in a harnessed car seat while still strapped in it; the seat keeps the spine aligned. Older children in boosters may climb out with a collar on.

questions.stem: An adult with severe asthma is getting nebulized albuterol. Which medication is often added to it?
questions.explanation: Ipratropium, an anticholinergic, works with albuterol to open the airways in a severe attack and is within AEMT scope by protocol. Diphenhydramine treats itching and hives, not bronchospasm.

questions.stem: Sudden tearing chest pain spreads to the back, and the BP is 30 mm Hg higher in the right arm. What fits?
questions.explanation: Tearing pain to the back with unequal arm pressures suggests aortic dissection, where aspirin can worsen bleeding. He needs gentle handling and rapid transport, not exertion or large fluid volumes.

questions.stem: The head has delivered but the body will not follow with pushing. What should you try first?
options: Flex her hips sharply to her chest
Push on the top of the belly
Pull down hard on the head
questions.explanation: Shoulder dystocia is treated by hyperflexing the mother's hips (McRoberts maneuver), with firm pressure just above the pubic bone if needed. Never pull on the head or push on the fundus.

questions.stem: Place the steps for preparing an IV bag and tubing in order.
options: Run fluid to clear the tubing
Squeeze to fill the drip chamber
questions.explanation: Check the bag first, close the clamp so fluid does not run out when you spike, fill the drip chamber about halfway, then flush the line to clear air before it goes near the patient.

questions.stem: For each patient, specify whether an early 12-lead ECG should be acquired.
rows: Age 72 with diabetes, weak and short of breath
questions.explanation: Chest pain, atypical symptoms in older or diabetic patients and syncope can all be ACS or an arrhythmia, so a 12-lead is acquired early. An ankle sprain or sore throat gives no reason for one.

questions.stem: Before suctioning a patient's tracheostomy tube, what should you do?
options: Insert the catheter with suction on
questions.explanation: Suctioning removes oxygen along with secretions, so preoxygenate first. Suction is applied only while withdrawing the catheter, and the cuff and inner cannula are left alone unless the tube is blocked.

questions.stem: Which wounds need an occlusive dressing? Select two.
options: Large cut over a neck vein
questions.explanation: Open chest wounds can let air into the chest, and open neck veins can draw in air that travels to the heart, so both are sealed. Limb wounds are dressed and pressed.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected sepsis has a BP of 96/60. What is the MAP, in mm Hg?
questions.explanation: NASEMSO calculates MAP as (2 x diastolic + systolic) / 3: (120 + 96) / 3 = 72 mm Hg, above the 65 target for septic shock.

questions.stem: Place the steps for giving a medication in order.
questions.explanation: Confirm the indication and order, check allergies, verify the drug, dose, route and expiration, give it, then reassess the effect and record it. Documenting before giving invites errors.

questions.stem: A woman 34 weeks pregnant has a BP of 168/112. Which findings suggest severe preeclampsia? Select three.
questions.explanation: Headache, visual changes and right upper quadrant pain with high blood pressure point to severe preeclampsia, which can progress to seizures. A slow pulse, borderline glucose and mild fever do not.

questions.passage: HR 48, BP 88/56, RR 20, SpO2 95%. Lungs clear. Skin cool and diaphoretic.
questions.stem: Which findings need attention right away? Select three.
questions.explanation: A slow heart rate, low blood pressure and cool, sweaty skin show the heart is not pumping enough. A normal saturation, clear lungs and a normal rate are reassuring.

questions.stem: Which action comes first?
questions.explanation: Chest pain with these findings needs a 12-lead within minutes so a STEMI can be found and the PCI center alerted. Nitroglycerin is unsafe at this pressure and exertion strains his heart.

questions.stem: The PCI center reads an inferior STEMI and, with clear lungs, advises a small fluid bolus. Why?
options: It dilutes the clot in the artery
questions.explanation: Inferior infarcts often injure the right ventricle, which needs enough return of blood to pump. A small bolus with clear lungs can raise the pressure.

questions.stem: For this patient, specify whether each intervention is indicated.
questions.explanation: Aspirin, a cautious bolus and direct transport to the PCI center help him. Nitroglycerin is withheld with SBP under 100, and walking adds strain to an injured heart.

questions.stem: Which detail in your radio report helps the PCI center most?
questions.explanation: The time of symptom onset guides reperfusion decisions, along with the ECG and vital signs. The rest does not change his care.

questions.stem: En route he becomes unresponsive with no pulse. What do you do?
options: Pull over and wait for ALS
questions.explanation: Start high-quality compressions at once and attach the AED; an early shock for a shockable rhythm is the most important intervention. Glucose and other checks wait.

questions.stem: Place the steps for starting CPAP on an alert patient in order.
options: Hold the mask on gently at first
Explain it and check the BP
questions.explanation: Coaching and a BP check come first, then let the patient feel the mask before strapping it, start low and adjust while watching breathing, saturation and blood pressure.

questions.stem: Which drugs does the national scope model allow AEMTs to give IV? Select two.
questions.explanation: The scope model limits AEMT IV drugs to analgesia, antiemetics, dextrose, epinephrine, glucagon, naloxone and others set by state protocol. Amiodarone, midazolam and adenosine are paramedic drugs.

questions.stem: An alert COPD patient has an SpO2 of 91 percent and mild distress. What is the best oxygen approach?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is a drug with a dose: patients with chronic lung disease often do well at a saturation around 90 percent, and high flows can worsen CO2 retention. Withholding it is also wrong when the patient is hypoxic.

questions.stem: For each patient, specify whether a cervical collar and spinal motion restriction are indicated.
rows: Smells of alcohol after a crash
Tingling in both hands after a dive
Alert, sober, no pain or deficit
Stab wound to the side of the neck
Midline neck tenderness after a fall
questions.explanation: Midline tenderness, intoxication and neurologic signs call for a collar. An alert, sober patient with no pain or deficit does not need one, and a penetrating neck wound should not be collared because it hides bleeding and airway swelling.

questions.stem: A newborn is dried and stimulated but his heart rate is 80. What next?
questions.explanation: A heart rate under 100 after drying and stimulation means the baby needs positive pressure ventilation. Compressions start only if the rate stays under 60 despite good ventilation.

questions.stem: After ROSC, how should you ventilate a patient who is not breathing on his own?
options: As fast as the bag refills
To an ETCO2 under 25 mm Hg
questions.explanation: After ROSC, aim for normal ventilation: an ETCO2 of 35 to 45 mm Hg and an SpO2 in the 90s. Hyperventilation lowers CO2, narrows brain vessels and reduces return of blood to the heart.

questions.stem: At a chemical spill, where should an AEMT treat decontaminated patients?
questions.explanation: Patient care happens in the cold zone after decontamination in the warm zone. The hot zone is for trained hazmat teams, and downwind exposes the crew.

questions.stem: During newborn resuscitation, what ratio of compressions to breaths is used?
questions.explanation: Newborns get coordinated compressions and breaths at 3:1, since their arrests are almost always from lack of oxygen. 15:2 is for two-rescuer child CPR and 30:2 for adults.

questions.stem: Which findings show an adult needs assisted ventilation? Select three.
questions.explanation: A slow, shallow rate, a rising ETCO2 and falling mental status with cyanosis all show the patient is not moving enough air. Full sentences, a good saturation and pursed-lip breathing show the patient is still compensating.

questions.stem: During labor the cord is seen in the vagina ahead of the baby. What should you do?
options: Hold the baby off the cord
questions.explanation: With a gloved hand, hold the baby's presenting part off the cord to keep blood flowing, cover the cord with moist sterile gauze, and raise her hips or use knee-chest position during rapid transport.

questions.stem: A patient with HR 36 is pale and hypotensive. Which treatment is outside AEMT scope?
questions.explanation: Transcutaneous pacing, like manual defibrillation and cardioversion, is a paramedic skill in the national scope model. An AEMT can give oxygen, start an IV, acquire the 12-lead and request ALS.

questions.stem: How should an amputated finger be prepared for transport?
options: Soaked in a cup of saline
Bagged dry, bag set on ice
questions.explanation: NASEMSO keeps the part cool but dry: in a plastic bag, which then sits on ice inside a second bag. Direct contact with ice or water damages the tissue.

questions.stem: A woman bleeding early in pregnancy has passed tissue. What should you do with it?
questions.explanation: Tissue passed during a miscarriage is placed in a container or bag and brought with her so the hospital can examine it. Treat her for blood loss and offer emotional support.

questions.passage: Temperature 38.9 C, HR 118, RR 28, BP 86/48, SpO2 93%. She knows her name but not where she is.
questions.stem: Which explanation best fits?
questions.explanation: Fever, fast heart and breathing rates, low blood pressure and new confusion during a known infection point to sepsis. Dementia does not cause fever or low blood pressure.

questions.stem: Which information from the staff matters most for the hospital?
options: Which aide is on shift today
questions.explanation: Knowing she normally talks in full sentences shows today's confusion is new, which is key to recognizing sepsis. Ask the staff and record their description.

questions.stem: NASEMSO's fluid goal for adult septic shock is up to 30 mL/kg. What is the most she would get, in mL?
questions.explanation: 30 mL/kg x 60 kg = 1,800 mL, given in rapid boluses such as 500 mL and stopped early if the MAP reaches 65 or her lungs fill with fluid.

questions.passage: After 1,000 mL: BP 98/58, MAP 71, HR 104. New crackles at both lung bases; SpO2 89%.
questions.stem: What should you do about the fluid now?
options: Speed the IV to wide open
Give the rest of the fluid
questions.explanation: Her pressure has reached the goal, and new crackles with a falling saturation mean her failing heart is not handling more fluid. Stop the bolus and support her breathing.

questions.stem: She is alert with crackles and an SpO2 of 89 percent. What helps her breathing most simply?
questions.explanation: Raising the head of the stretcher and giving oxygen to an SpO2 of 94 to 98 percent eases her breathing. Lying flat lets fluid move into more of the lungs.

questions.stem: Which phrase best alerts the receiving hospital?
questions.explanation: Naming suspected sepsis and hypotension lets the hospital prepare for antibiotics and cultures on arrival. Vague phrases delay that.

questions.stem: What is the safest way to back up an ambulance?
questions.explanation: Backing is a common cause of ambulance collisions. A spotter at the rear, kept in view in the mirror, sees the blind spots that mirrors leave.

questions.stem: Late in pregnancy, which finding points to placental abruption rather than previa?
questions.explanation: Abruption, where the placenta tears away from the wall, causes pain and a tense uterus, and bleeding may be hidden. Placenta previa typically bleeds bright red without pain.

questions.stem: A drooling 6-year-old with a high fever is sitting forward and will not lie down. What should you avoid?
questions.explanation: These are signs of epiglottitis, and a tongue blade or a forced position can trigger complete obstruction. Keep the child calm and upright with a parent and give oxygen she will tolerate.

questions.stem: A patient with an LVAD is alert and talking, but you cannot feel a pulse. How do you judge perfusion?
questions.explanation: Continuous-flow LVADs often leave no palpable pulse, so an alert patient with warm, dry skin is perfusing. Listen for the pump hum, check for alarms and call the VAD coordinator whose number is on the device.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman with high BP has a seizure. Which drug treats eclamptic seizures, given by ALS?
questions.explanation: Magnesium sulfate treats and prevents eclamptic seizures and is a paramedic-level drug. The AEMT protects her from injury, positions her on her left side and gets ALS en route.

questions.stem: Bowel protrudes from a deep abdominal cut. What is the right care?
options: Leave it open to the air
questions.explanation: Cover the organs with moist sterile dressing and an occlusive layer to keep them moist and warm. Pushing them back adds contamination, and dry gauze sticks to the tissue.

questions.stem: Which finding fits diabetic ketoacidosis?
questions.explanation: In DKA the body blows off acid as CO2 with deep, rapid Kussmaul breaths, often with fruity breath and dehydration. Cool, sweaty skin is more typical of low blood sugar.

questions.stem: Which patient is most likely to have a heart attack with no chest pain at all?
questions.explanation: Older adults, people with diabetes and women often present with weakness, shortness of breath or nausea instead of chest pain. Smoking raises risk but does not make the pain atypical.

questions.stem: During BVM ventilation the patient's abdomen swells. What most often causes this?
options: Breaths too fast or too big
A jaw thrust held too firmly
An oral airway sized too small
questions.explanation: Large or rapid breaths open the esophagus and push air into the stomach, raising the risk of vomiting and aspiration. Slow breaths of just enough volume to raise the chest prevent it.

questions.stem: Which drug is used for nausea and vomiting within AEMT protocols?
questions.explanation: Ondansetron is an antiemetic, a class the scope model lets AEMTs give IV by protocol. NASEMSO avoids it in patients with a known prolonged QT interval.

questions.stem: Which entry is written correctly for a patient care report?
questions.explanation: Reports record what you see, hear and smell, not labels or opinions. Objective findings protect the patient and the crew; judgments can be wrong and look biased.

questions.stem: A self-administered nitrous oxide mask would be unsafe for which patient?
questions.explanation: Nitrous oxide expands into trapped air spaces, so a possible pneumothorax or bowel obstruction rules it out. Alert patients with painful injuries who can hold the mask are the usual candidates.

questions.passage: HR 124, BP 84/52, RR 26, audible wheeze, hoarse voice.
questions.stem: Which findings show this is anaphylaxis, not a mild reaction? Select three.
questions.explanation: Hoarseness, wheezing and low blood pressure show the reaction has reached the airway and circulation. Hives and itching occur in mild reactions too, and the exposure alone does not show severity.

questions.stem: Which drug and route come first?
questions.explanation: Epinephrine 0.3 mg of the 1 mg/mL strength, IM in the outer thigh, is the first treatment for anaphylaxis in an adult. The 1 mg/mL strength must never be pushed IV, and antihistamines and albuterol are add-ons.

questions.stem: She stays hypotensive after epinephrine. At NASEMSO's 20 mL/kg, what bolus volume in mL fits her weight?
questions.explanation: 20 mL/kg x 70 kg = 1,400 mL of isotonic fluid, given rapidly, while IM epinephrine can be repeated every 5 to 15 minutes.

questions.stem: Her BP is now 106/68, but she is still wheezing. What may be added?
questions.explanation: NASEMSO adds nebulized albuterol for wheezing in anaphylaxis once epinephrine is given. Nitroglycerin would drop the pressure that has just recovered.

questions.stem: She feels better and asks why she still has to go to the hospital. What do you tell her?
options: She needs an allergy skin test
questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis can recur after the epinephrine wears off, sometimes hours later, so she needs observation. Honest reasons help her agree to go.

questions.stem: Your EMT partner is about to inject the next dose into her upper arm. What should you say?
options: The arm is fine; go ahead
questions.explanation: The anterolateral thigh absorbs IM epinephrine faster and more reliably, which is why guidelines name it. Speaking up clearly is part of leading the crew.

questions.stem: A rod is impaled in a patient's thigh and the airway is clear. What should you do with it?
options: Pull it out to stop bleeding
Cut it flush with the skin
questions.explanation: An impaled object is stabilized in place with bulky dressings because it may be plugging the bleeding it caused. Removal is only for an object blocking the airway or chest compressions.

questions.stem: Why transmit a 12-lead showing a possible STEMI before arrival?
options: The center can ready its cath lab
It replaces the hospital's own ECG
It is required to give aspirin
questions.explanation: Advance notification lets a PCI center activate its team so the artery opens sooner. AEMTs do not give thrombolytics, and aspirin does not wait for an ECG.

questions.stem: A patient vomits dark material that looks like coffee grounds. What does it suggest?
questions.explanation: Blood that sits in the stomach turns dark and grainy, so coffee-ground vomit points to bleeding in the upper GI tract. Watch for signs of shock and save a description.

questions.stem: ETCO2 suddenly drops to zero in an apneic patient ventilated through a supraglottic airway. What should you suspect first?
questions.explanation: A sudden flat line means no CO2 is coming back, most often from a dislodged, kinked or disconnected airway. Check the device and tubing at once; hyperventilation lowers ETCO2 gradually, it does not erase it.

questions.stem: A patient from a house fire has a headache and an SpO2 of 99 percent. What oxygen does she need?
questions.explanation: NASEMSO gives high-flow oxygen to everyone rescued from an enclosed space fire. A normal SpO2 can hide carbon monoxide, and high oxygen speeds its removal.

questions.stem: Chest pain began while shoveling snow and went away with rest within 5 minutes. This pattern suggests:
questions.explanation: Pain brought on by exertion and relieved by rest is the classic pattern of stable angina. A dissection tears suddenly, pericarditis changes with position, and an embolism brings sudden shortness of breath.

questions.stem: An older woman you transport has bruises in many stages and seems afraid of her caregiver. What fits?
options: Report it only if she asks
questions.explanation: EMS providers are mandated reporters of suspected abuse in most states. Report through the required channel, document objective findings and avoid confronting the suspected abuser.

questions.stem: When a violent patient must be physically restrained, which position must never be used?
options: On the side with straps across
Supine with all four limbs held
questions.explanation: Prone, face down or hog-tied restraint can stop a patient from breathing and has caused deaths. Restrain supine or on the side and watch breathing closely.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old on a blood thinner fell from standing and hit her head. She seems fine. Why is she high risk?
questions.explanation: Anticoagulants make delayed bleeding inside the skull more likely after even a low fall, so the 2022 field triage guideline flags these patients for trauma center care. A normal first exam does not rule it out.

questions.stem: When is a Venturi mask the best oxygen device?
options: When a precise FiO2 is needed
When the patient breathes by mouth
When the patient needs maximum oxygen
questions.explanation: A Venturi mask mixes air and oxygen through a fixed port to give an exact concentration, useful in chronic lung disease. Apnea needs a BVM, and a nonrebreather gives the most oxygen to a breathing patient.

questions.stem: A hiker was bitten on the ankle by a rattlesnake. What is right?
options: Tie a band above the bite
questions.explanation: NASEMSO forbids tourniquets, constricting bands, incision, suction and ice for envenomation. Keep the limb still, remove rings and tight items and transport to a center with antivenom.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old athlete fainted while sprinting and recovered quickly. Why is this concerning?
options: It is a sign of dehydration
questions.explanation: Fainting during exertion, unlike fainting after standing up, can come from a structural heart problem or an arrhythmia and needs a cardiac workup. Dehydration usually causes fainting after effort or when standing.

questions.stem: A swimmer pulled from a pool is pulseless. What does resuscitation emphasize?
questions.explanation: Drowning arrests come from lack of oxygen, so early rescue breaths are central along with compressions. Abdominal thrusts delay CPR and do not remove water from the lungs.

questions.stem: As the first crew on scene, what should you do first?
options: Start CPR on the van patient
questions.explanation: Six patients outnumber one crew, so the first job is scene size-up, a call for more resources and starting triage. Treating one patient first leaves the rest unsorted.

questions.stem: Your system uses SALT triage. Place the global sort and first steps in order.
options: Ask the rest to wave or move
Ask those who can walk to move
questions.explanation: SALT sorts first: walkers are assessed last, wavers next, and those who are still or have obvious threats first. Quick lifesaving steps such as bleeding control come before each patient is categorized.

questions.stem: Assign each patient a SALT category.
rows: Open fracture, obeys, radial pulse, no distress
In the van, no breathing after airway opened
In the road, in respiratory distress
Walking, small cuts to the arms
questions.explanation: Minor injuries go to minimal, respiratory distress makes a patient immediate, and an adult who does not breathe after the airway is opened is dead in SALT. A patient who obeys, has a pulse and no distress but has a serious fracture is delayed.

questions.stem: Which message to dispatch is most useful?
questions.explanation: A clear report of how many patients, how many are immediate and what resources you need lets dispatch send the right help. Vague or open-ended requests waste units.

questions.stem: A second ambulance arrives with two EMTs. How should you use them?
options: Have them treat the minor patients
questions.explanation: Give clear assignments to the patients who need care most, the immediate ones. Minor patients can wait or be watched by fewer people.

questions.stem: A walking patient you tagged minimal is now pale, sweaty and confused. What should you do?
questions.explanation: Triage is repeated because patients change. New signs of shock and altered mental status move him to immediate.

questions.stem: You are stuck by a used needle while starting an IV. What comes first?
questions.explanation: Wash the site with soap and water at once, then report the exposure right away so testing and preventive treatment can start in time. Bleach and squeezing do not help.

questions.stem: A man who smells of alcohol is found confused on a sidewalk. Why not assume he is just drunk?
options: Low sugar or a head injury can mimic it
questions.explanation: Hypoglycemia, a head injury, a stroke or an overdose can all look like intoxication, and alcohol makes them easier to miss. Check glucose, look for trauma and assess fully.

questions.stem: A woman 30 weeks pregnant is strapped flat to a long board and becomes dizzy and pale. What helps?
options: Put her legs up on pillows
Raise the head end of the board
Tilt the board to her left
questions.explanation: Lying flat lets the uterus press on the vena cava and cut blood return to the heart. Tilting the whole board to the left, or displacing the uterus by hand, relieves it.

questions.stem: A patient on a home ventilator through a tracheostomy is in distress and the alarm sounds. What first?
questions.explanation: When a ventilated patient is struggling, take the machine out of the equation: disconnect it and bag through the tracheostomy, then look for displacement, obstruction or a pneumothorax.

questions.stem: After a nitroglycerin tablet, the patient says his head pounds. What explains this?
questions.explanation: Nitroglycerin dilates vessels, including those in the head, so a throbbing headache is a common, expected effect. Recheck the BP because the same dilation can cause hypotension.

questions.stem: A man is in the middle of a generalized seizure on a tile floor. What should you do?
options: Put a bite block between his teeth
Hold his arms and legs still
Move hard objects away from him
questions.explanation: Protect him from injury and time the seizure. Nothing goes in the mouth, holding the limbs can cause fractures, and oral glucose is unsafe while he is seizing.

questions.stem: Each adult has a glucose under 60 mg/dL. Specify the right treatment route.
rows: Confused but can sip and swallow
questions.explanation: Oral glucose is for a conscious patient with a patent airway. A patient who is unresponsive or seizing needs IV dextrose, or IM or IN glucagon when no IV can be placed.

questions.stem: For each adult in respiratory distress, specify whether CPAP is appropriate.
rows: Sudden chest pain, absent breath sounds on one side
questions.explanation: Alert patients with pulmonary edema or a COPD flare who can keep a mask on benefit from CPAP. An unprotected airway, hypotension and a suspected pneumothorax are contraindications.

questions.stem: Which findings point toward aortic dissection rather than a heart attack? Select two.
options: Arm pressures differ by 25 mm Hg
Tearing pain that goes to the back
questions.explanation: Sudden tearing pain radiating to the back and unequal arm pressures suggest a dissection. Relief by leaning forward points to pericarditis, and pain reproduced by palpation suggests a chest wall cause.

questions.stem: A 100 kg adult has burns over about 30 percent of the body and is not in shock. Using the Rule of 10, what is the starting fluid rate in mL per hour?
questions.explanation: 30 x 10 = 300 mL per hour for the burns, then add 100 mL per hour for each 10 kg over 80 kg: 100 kg is 20 kg over, so 300 + 200 = 500 mL per hour.

questions.stem: Which elements are needed for a patient's refusal to be valid? Select two.
questions.explanation: A valid refusal needs a patient with capacity who has been told and understands the risks of refusing. A relative's agreement or a police signature does not make it valid.

questions.stem: Place the steps for starting a peripheral IV in order.
options: Insert bevel up; watch for flash
Apply the tourniquet; pick a vein
questions.explanation: Find the vein under a tourniquet, prepare the skin, enter bevel up until blood flashes, slide the catheter in and release the tourniquet before removing the needle, then connect and confirm free flow.

questions.stem: You must give 300 mL over 60 minutes with a 10 drop/mL set. How many drops per minute?
questions.explanation: Drops per minute = volume x drop factor / minutes: 300 x 10 / 60 = 50 drops per minute.

questions.stem: An oral airway should only be inserted in a patient who:
questions.explanation: An oral airway in a patient with a gag reflex can cause vomiting and aspiration. A patient who follows commands protects his own airway, and a neck injury does not decide the choice.

questions.stem: Where is the V4 electrode placed?
options: 4th intercostal space, right of the sternum
questions.explanation: V4 sits in the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line, V5 at the anterior axillary line on that level and V6 at the midaxillary line.

questions.stem: In an adult, how much body surface does one whole arm plus the front of the torso cover?
questions.explanation: By the Rule of Nines one arm is 9 percent and the front of the torso is 18 percent, so together they are 27 percent. Only partial and full thickness burns count toward the total.

questions.stem: The skin around an IV site is swollen, cool and pale, and the drip has slowed. What should you do?
questions.explanation: Swelling, coolness and pallor show the fluid is going into the tissue. Stop the infusion, remove the catheter and start a new line in another site; flushing pushes more fluid out of the vein.

questions.stem: What makes the best hospital handoff?
options: The chart left on the bed
questions.explanation: A brief structured format, such as mechanism, injuries, signs and treatment, keeps key facts from being missed. Leaving only paperwork or listing every detail loses the message.

questions.stem: What time should you report as her last known well?
questions.explanation: Her husband saw her normal right up to 0745, when the symptoms began, so that is both her onset time and her last known well. 0600 is when she woke, and 0820 is the call.

questions.passage: Right facial droop, right arm drift, garbled speech; she cannot find words and ignores things on her right. BP 178/96, glucose 118 mg/dL, SpO2 96%.
questions.stem: Which findings on a stroke severity screen suggest a large vessel occlusion? Select two.
questions.explanation: Severity scales look for cortical signs such as neglect of one side, aphasia and vision changes, which point to a large vessel stroke. High BP and a normal glucose are expected findings.

questions.stem: Her systolic pressure is 178. How should the stretcher be set?
questions.explanation: NASEMSO raises the head 15 to 30 degrees when SBP is over 100 to lower aspiration risk, with the neck kept straight. Legs-up or head-down positions are for shock.

questions.stem: Within protocol times, which destination fits a likely large vessel stroke?
questions.explanation: NASEMSO advises considering a center that can remove the clot for a positive severity screen within 24 hours of last known well, as the local stroke plan allows.

questions.stem: Her medicine list includes apixaban. Why report it early?
options: It must be given before arrival
questions.explanation: Anticoagulant use is pertinent history in suspected stroke because it changes whether clot-dissolving drugs are safe. Reporting it early speeds the stroke team's decisions.

questions.stem: Her husband is the only witness. What is best?
options: Bring him or get his number
Have him drive behind you fast
Ask him to call her doctor
questions.explanation: The hospital team needs the witness for the timeline and decisions, so NASEMSO advises bringing him or getting a number they can call.

questions.stem: After 2 L of saline an older patient has new crackles and worse breathing. What do you suspect?
questions.explanation: Crackles and rising distress after large volumes show fluid backing up into the lungs. Slow the IV to keep-open, sit the patient up and report it.

questions.stem: Which finding rules out the proximal tibia as an IO site?
questions.explanation: IO needles are not placed in a fractured bone, a site with infection, or a bone with a recent IO attempt, because fluid leaks out. Shock and arrest with no IV access are why IO is used.

questions.stem: What volume should each BVM breath deliver to an adult?
options: Enough to make the belly rise
Enough to see the chest rise
questions.explanation: Guidelines call for about 6 to 8 mL/kg, which is the volume that makes the chest start to rise. Squeezing the whole bag raises chest pressure, lowers blood return to the heart and fills the stomach.

questions.stem: Why keep the pause before an AED shock as short as possible?
options: The AED cannot analyze after a pause
Long pauses drain the AED battery
questions.explanation: Blood flow to the heart builds slowly during compressions and drops quickly when they stop, so long pauses make a shock less likely to work. Battery and pad temperature are not the reason.

questions.stem: A worker's leg has been pinned under a beam for 3 hours. What should happen before the beam is lifted?
options: A tourniquet placed and left on
questions.explanation: Releasing a crushed limb floods the blood with potassium and acid, so NASEMSO starts normal saline before release. Lactated Ringer's is avoided because it contains potassium.

questions.stem: An unresponsive adult needs care and no family is present. Which consent applies?
questions.explanation: The law assumes an unresponsive person would agree to emergency care, so implied consent applies. Expressed consent comes from a patient who can speak for himself.

questions.stem: When is IM glucagon the best choice for a hypoglycemic adult?
options: When no IV can be placed
When the patient can eat a meal
questions.explanation: NASEMSO uses glucagon 1 mg IM or IN when an IV cannot be started. A patient who can swallow gets oral glucose, and treatment follows a glucose check.

questions.stem: An altered patient with an insulin pump has a glucose of 38. ALS is far away and he cannot swallow. What about the pump?
questions.explanation: NASEMSO stops, disconnects or removes the pump when the patient cannot take oral glucose and ALS is not available, so it stops delivering insulin. A patient who can eat keeps it running.

questions.stem: A patient stung by a wasp has stridor and hives. What treats the stridor first?
questions.explanation: Stridor in anaphylaxis is upper airway swelling, and IM epinephrine is the first treatment. Albuterol helps wheezing, not upper airway edema, and an antihistamine works too slowly.

questions.stem: When is a mechanical CPR device most helpful?
options: While moving him to the ambulance
In the first minute of a witnessed arrest
When the AED advises a shock
questions.explanation: A device keeps compressions steady on stairs and in a moving ambulance, where manual CPR is poor and unsafe. Applying it should not delay early compressions or a shock.

questions.stem: Which finding defines a flail chest segment?
options: It moves in as he breathes in
It bulges out as he breathes in
questions.explanation: A flail segment is two or more ribs broken in two or more places, so it is sucked inward on inhalation, the opposite of the rest of the chest. Crepitus alone shows a fracture, not a flail.

questions.stem: A patient in cardiac arrest has a valid DNR order at the bedside. What is appropriate?
options: Start CPR until a doctor arrives
questions.explanation: A valid DNR means resuscitation is withheld, while you still offer comfort and support to the family. Confirm the document follows your state's rules and local protocol.

questions.stem: After IM epinephrine, a patient with anaphylaxis still has a BP of 80/50. What should be added?
questions.explanation: NASEMSO adds 20 mL/kg of isotonic fluid given rapidly for poor perfusion in anaphylaxis and repeats IM epinephrine every 5 to 15 minutes.

questions.stem: A woman of childbearing age has lower abdominal pain. Which question is most important early?
questions.explanation: Any woman who could be pregnant with abdominal pain may have an ectopic pregnancy, so the last menstrual period guides the assessment.

questions.stem: A teen in diabetic ketoacidosis is breathing deep and fast, with an ETCO2 of 20 mm Hg. What does the low reading reflect?
questions.explanation: In DKA the body compensates for acid by blowing off CO2, so ETCO2 falls well below the normal 35 to 45 mm Hg. Do not try to slow this breathing; it is the patient's own correction.

questions.stem: After a large heart attack, BP is 80/50 with crackles in both lungs. What fits the fluid plan?
questions.explanation: A failing heart cannot handle large volumes, so any fluid goes in small boluses with frequent lung checks, while ALS and the receiving center are alerted. Withholding IV access removes a route for ALS drugs.

questions.stem: A 20 kg child with trauma has poor perfusion. What is the first fluid bolus?
questions.explanation: Children with signs of shock get 20 mL/kg of crystalloid, here 400 mL, then reassessment before any repeat. Smaller 10 mL/kg boluses are kept for children in cardiogenic shock.

questions.stem: A teen with sickle cell disease has pain. Which finding is most urgent?
options: Chest pain, fever and low SpO2
questions.explanation: Chest pain with fever, cough or low oxygen in sickle cell disease suggests acute chest syndrome, a leading cause of death in these patients. Joint pain is the common crisis.

questions.stem: Which act could be called abandonment?
options: Leaving him with an EMR without a report
Handing over to a paramedic with a report
questions.explanation: Abandonment is ending care without transferring it to someone with equal or higher training. A documented transfer or a valid refusal is not abandonment.

questions.passage: The baby's head is visible at the vaginal opening with each contraction.
questions.stem: Should you transport now or prepare to deliver?
options: Have her walk to the ambulance
Ask her to cross her legs
questions.explanation: Crowning with strong contractions in a woman with prior births means birth is minutes away, far less than the 40-minute drive. Delivering in a controlled setting is safer than in a moving ambulance.

questions.stem: The baby is born limp. After drying and stimulating, how do you check his heart rate best?
questions.explanation: Listening over the chest gives a fast, accurate newborn heart rate; feeling the cord base works but often undercounts. A radial pulse is not reliable in a newborn, and oximetry takes time to read.

questions.stem: While you wait for the placenta, specify whether each finding is a sign it is separating.
questions.explanation: A lengthening cord, a small gush of blood and a uterus that firms and rises mean the placenta is separating. Never pull on the cord to speed it.

questions.passage: Ten minutes after the placenta delivers she is bleeding steadily. The uterus feels soft. HR 118, BP 96/60.
questions.stem: Besides fundal massage, what helps the uterus contract?
questions.explanation: Nursing releases oxytocin, which makes the uterus contract. Packing and pulling on the cord can cause serious injury.

questions.stem: Bleeding continues and her BP falls to 88/50. What else should you do?
options: Wait on scene for it to stop
Seat her upright in a chair
questions.explanation: Ongoing bleeding with falling pressure needs IV access, fluid toward a palpable pulse, continued massage and rapid transport. Waiting on scene lets the blood loss grow.

questions.stem: Which details matter most in your radio report?
questions.explanation: The receiving team needs the time of birth, estimated blood loss, her vital signs and the newborn's condition to prepare. The rest can wait.

questions.stem: A mildly hypothermic hiker is shivering and alert. What helps first?
questions.explanation: Remove wet clothing, dry him and wrap him in blankets in a warm space. Alcohol widens vessels and speeds heat loss, and exertion or rubbing can stress a cold heart.

questions.stem: Which finding separates heat stroke from heat exhaustion?
questions.explanation: Confusion, seizures or unresponsiveness with a high temperature mark heat stroke. Sweating, cramps and fatigue occur in heat exhaustion, and some heat stroke patients still sweat.

questions.stem: While suctioning a vomiting patient, when should suction be applied?
questions.explanation: Suction is applied as the tip is withdrawn and kept brief, about 15 seconds or less in an adult, with oxygen between passes. Rolling the patient onto the side first lets gravity clear most of the vomit.

questions.stem: Where should a patient with a transmitted STEMI usually be taken?
questions.explanation: A center that can open the artery in the cath lab shortens time to reperfusion. Urgent care centers and offices cannot treat a STEMI, so the patient would need a second transfer.

questions.stem: Once the burning has stopped, how does NASEMSO advise covering a large burn?
questions.explanation: Cover burns with a dry dressing or a clean sheet to limit contamination and heat loss, and leave blisters intact. Gels and ointments are avoided, and wet coverings over a large area chill the patient.

questions.stem: How should you lift a loaded stretcher?
options: Keep it close; use your legs
Bend at the waist; lift fast
questions.explanation: Keep the load close, back straight, and lift with the legs. Twisting or reaching while holding weight is a common cause of back injury in EMS.

questions.stem: Right after birth a newborn is breathing and crying. What comes next?
questions.explanation: Newborns lose heat fast, so dry, warm and keep them skin to skin. Routine deep suctioning is not needed for a baby who is breathing and crying.
